notes.meaning: Baasha, the king of the northern kingdom of Israel, blocked the main highway into Judah by fortifying Ramah, just a few miles north of Jerusalem. He wanted to trap his own people and prevent them from traveling south to join Asa and worship the true God. This hostile move put Judah under heavy economic and military pressure.

Instead of crying out to the Lord for help, King Asa emptied out the treasures of the temple and his own palace. He sent this wealth as a bribe to King Ben-hadad of Aram in Damascus. Asa chose to spend sacred wealth dedicated to God to purchase the protection of a pagan king.

Asa appealed to past peace treaties made by their fathers to convince Ben-hadad to become his ally. He urged the Syrian king to break his existing treaty with Baasha so that Israel would back off from Judah. Asa was encouraging another ruler to break his word, placing his trust in deceitful diplomacy rather than God's covenant promises.

Ben-hadad accepted the bribe and sent his armies to attack northern Israel. His forces overran several cities and food storage centers in the territory of Naphtali. On the surface, Asa's political scheme succeeded right away by forcing Israel to defend its own borders.

When Baasha heard that Syria had attacked his northern land, he immediately stopped building the fortress at Ramah. He abandoned his materials and rushed home to defend his kingdom. Humanly speaking, the danger to Judah was gone, but Asa had secured relief without turning to God.

King Asa called together all the men of Judah to haul away the stones and timbers Baasha had left behind at Ramah. He used those very building supplies to fortify his own border towns, Geba and Mizpah. He turned the enemy's abandoned siege post into strong defense points to protect his own kingdom.

The prophet Hanani arrived with a direct rebuke from God for King Asa. He told Asa that because he had leaned on the king of Aram instead of the Lord his God, the Syrian army had escaped his grasp. If Asa had trusted God, the Lord would have given him victory over both Israel and Syria together.

Hanani reminded Asa of an earlier battle against an enormous army of Cushites and Libyans. Even though that enemy had countless horsemen and chariots, the Lord handed them over because Asa trusted Him. God had already proved His mighty power, which made Asa's current lack of faith inexcusable.

Hanani declared that the Lord constantly watches over the whole earth, eager to show His mighty strength for anyone whose heart is fully loyal to Him. Asa had acted foolishly by trusting in money and human treaties instead of God. Because he walked away from faith, his long season of peace ended, and he would face constant warfare.

Instead of humbling himself and repenting, King Asa flew into a rage at the prophet. He locked Hanani in prison stocks and began mistreating some of his own people who likely sympathized with the prophet's message. Refusing to accept God's correction hardened Asa's heart and led him into outright tyranny.

The writer notes that the complete record of Asa's life and reign was preserved in the royal history books of Judah and Israel. Those court records preserved every detail of his accomplishments and his later failures from beginning to end.

Near the close of his reign, Asa developed a severe and painful disease in his feet. Even when his illness grew worse, he refused to seek the Lord in prayer, relying entirely on physicians instead. Consulting doctors was not wrong, but relying on human skill while completely ignoring God showed how far his faith had fallen.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some commentators suggest Asa's physicians were foreign practitioners who used magical charms and incantations rather than ordinary medicine, making his reliance on them even worse.

notes.meaning: King Asa died in the forty-first year of his reign and rested with his ancestors. His rule had started with great spiritual renewal, but it ended in physical torment and spiritual decline. His life serves as a warning that starting well is not enough if one does not stay faithful to the end.

The people buried Asa in the rock-cut tomb he had prepared for himself in the City of David. They laid his body on a couch filled with fragrant spices and oils, and they burned a huge blaze of sweet spices in his honor. In spite of his late failures, his subjects remembered his earlier good deeds and gave him a grand royal funeral.
